passage:
The inter-school quiz prize was two thousand rupees, and Ujjwal had the envelope in his blazer by lunch. By the last bell, most of it was gone. He had bought cold drinks and samosas for the whole class at the canteen, a new pair of earphones, and a comic from the book fair in the school hall.
"You've spent it all?" Kishore asked, stuffing a samosa in his mouth.
"It was prize money, yaar. Free money."
"But you won't even buy a chai with your tuition money."
Ujjwal went quiet. He taught maths to two kids in his building every evening and kept that money folded in a book at home. "That's different. I earned that."
Kishore shrugged. "You earned the quiz too. You studied for weeks."

qa.q: What did Ujjwal buy for the whole class?
qa.a: He bought cold drinks and samosas for the whole class at the canteen.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal feel it was fine to spend the prize money so quickly?
qa.a: To Ujjwal the prize felt like "free money" for fun, unlike the tuition money he earned by teaching, so spending it felt guilt-free.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal try the next time he gets a windfall?
qa.a: Keep it for a few days before spending and ask whether he would spend the same amount from his tuition money; if not, he may want to slow down.

qa.q: How does Kishore see the difference Ujjwal is making?
qa.a: Kishore doesn't see much difference, since Ujjwal studied for weeks to win the quiz, so both sums were earned in their own way.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy spending a prize quickly as fun money while guarding money he earned, though each rupee is worth the same.

passage:
Dear Chinmay,
Guess what, I got my birthday money from Grandpa in Kochi: three thousand rupees! I spent it in one weekend. A football, two video games, pizza with the boys, and a hoodie I didn't really need. It felt great.
The weird thing is, I also have the money from my newspaper round. Four months of getting up at six. I haven't spent a single rupee of that. Last week I wanted new football boots and I didn't touch it. I kept thinking, that's real money.
My mum says money is money, and I know she's right. Every rupee buys the same stuff. But when it comes from a birthday card, it feels like it's for having fun, and when I earn it, it feels like it's for something serious.
Are you like this too?
Your cousin brother,
Thomas

qa.q: How much birthday money did Thomas get from Grandpa?
qa.a: Thomas got three thousand rupees from Grandpa in Kochi.

qa.q: Why does the newspaper money feel like "real money" to Thomas?
qa.a: Thomas feels proud of the newspaper money because he earned it by getting up at six for four months, so he is careful with it, while the birthday money felt meant for fun.

qa.q: What would you advise Thomas about his next birthday money?
qa.a: Before spending, imagine it came from the newspaper round and ask if the purchase still feels worth it; that helps treat every rupee the same way.

qa.q: Why might Thomas's mum react differently to his spending?
qa.a: She sees all the money as the same, so she probably wishes he had been as careful with the birthday money as he is with his earnings.

grounding: It shows a teenager who spends gift money freely as fun money while guarding his earned money, though every rupee is the same.

passage:
Thomas, you asked what happened to the scholarship money, so here goes. I'm Noor, Abbu's eldest son, and I won the district essay prize in Class 10: four thousand rupees. My Abbu said, "Your prize, your choice." I was so happy I felt like I'd found treasure. In two weeks it was all gone: new shoes, gaming credits, treating my cousins to ice cream, and a phone cover I lost in a month.
Meanwhile, I'd been helping at my uncle's shop every Saturday, and I kept that money in an envelope under my mattress. I would never touch it. That was my serious money.
Now I look back and it's funny. The prize money was just as much mine. I even worked harder for it, rewriting that essay five times. My brain just filed it under fun.

qa.q: How much was Noor's district essay prize?
qa.a: The district essay prize was four thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why did Noor feel free to spend the prize money so fast?
qa.a: Winning it felt like finding treasure, so Noor's mind filed it under fun, while the shop money felt like serious money to protect.

qa.q: What could Noor do differently with a future prize?
qa.a: Put it in the same envelope as the shop money first, then decide calmly what to spend, since it was just as much Noor's and worked for just as hard.

qa.q: How might Noor's Abbu see how the prize money was spent?
qa.a: He gave Noor the choice, so he may accept it, though he might also wish some had lasted longer than a lost phone cover.

grounding: It shows a teenager who spent prize money quickly as fun money while guarding earned money, though all of it was equally the teenager's.

passage: I'm Suraj, Wasim's neighbour in the chawl. Wasim gets up at five every day to deliver newspapers, and he keeps that money in a steel box under his bed. He won't even buy a vada pav from it. "That's for my phone," he says. Last Sunday he won player of the match at the inter-colony cricket final: a thousand rupees in an envelope. By evening he had treated eight of us to falooda, bought new batting gloves and a cap he didn't need, and topped up his game credits. When I asked why he didn't put it in the steel box, he looked at me like I was mad. "Prize money is for enjoying, yaar." I don't know exactly what goes on in his head. But a rupee is a rupee, isn't it?

qa.q: Where does Wasim keep his newspaper money?
qa.a: In a steel box under his bed.

qa.q: Why does Wasim feel prize money is for enjoying while newspaper money isn't?
qa.a: The newspaper money comes from waking at five every day, so it feels earned and serious, while the prize arrived all at once and felt like a bonus for fun.

qa.q: What could Wasim do the next time he wins prize money?
qa.a: He could put part of it in the steel box before celebrating, so the prize also helps the phone he works so hard for.

qa.q: How might Suraj and the other friends see Wasim's falooda treat?
qa.a: They probably enjoyed it and saw Wasim as big-hearted, though Suraj also wonders why a prize rupee feels different to Wasim from an earned one 🤔

grounding: A neighbour watches a teenage boy guard his earned money but spend a prize in a day, as if the rupees were different.

passage:
Eid, Monday: Ayesha Khala pressed two thousand rupees into Irshad's hand. "Eidi, for you." By Wednesday he had spent most of it: a gaming headset, burgers for his cricket team and a pair of sunglasses. It felt light and easy, like money from nowhere.
The next Saturday: Irshad did his usual shift at his uncle's grocery, stacking rice bags, and was paid three hundred. His classmate Kavitha asked to borrow fifty for a notebook. "No way," he said. "I sweated for that."
Two weeks later: The school trip form came: eight hundred rupees. Irshad counted what was left: the three hundred in wages and forty rupees of Eidi. He stared at the sunglasses on his desk. "It was all the same money," he said out loud to the empty room.

qa.q: What did Irshad buy with the Eidi?
qa.a: A gaming headset, burgers for his cricket team and a pair of sunglasses.

qa.q: How did Irshad feel about his wages compared with the Eidi?
qa.a: Irshad felt protective of the wages he had sweated for and refused to lend any, while the Eidi felt light and easy, so he spent it in days.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Irshad, and what could he do differently next time?
qa.a: Counting his money for the trip form showed him that all rupees are the same; next time he could set aside part of any gift before spending.

qa.q: How might Kavitha have felt when Irshad refused fifty rupees?
qa.a: Kavitha may have felt hurt or surprised, having seen Irshad spend freely on burgers and sunglasses only days before.

grounding: A teenage boy spends gift money quickly while guarding his wages, until a trip form shows him every rupee counts the same.
